claim: The dataset consisted of 15 sessions of infant participants (4.8–23.1 months of age) who had both movie-watching data and retinotopic mapping data collected in the same session.
source: The dataset consisted of 15 sessions of infant participants (4.8–23.1 months of age) who had both movie-watching data and retinotopic mapping data collected in the same session (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset composition and participant characteristics.

claim: The average duration of movies shown to participants was 540.7 seconds with a range of 186–1116 seconds.
source: All available movies from each session were included (Appendix 1—table 2), with an average duration of 540.7 s (range: 186–1116 s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the movie stimulus duration.

claim: Retinotopic mapping data from the same infants allowed generation of infant-specific meridian maps and spatial frequency maps.
source: The retinotopic-mapping data from the same infants (Ellis et al., 2021) allowed us to generate infant-specific meridian maps (horizontal versus vertical stimulation) and spatial frequency maps (high versus low stimulation).
evidence: This statement describes the use of retinotopic mapping data from a prior study to generate specific types of maps.

claim: Meridian maps were used to define regions of interest for visual areas V1, V2, V3, V4, and V3A/B.
source: The meridian maps were used to define regions of interest (ROIs) for visual areas V1, V2, V3, V4, and V3A/B.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the use of meridian maps to define specific visual areas.

claim: An adult sample of 8 participants had both retinotopic mapping data and movie-watching data.
source: These adults (8 participants) had both retinotopic mapping data and movie-watching data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the adult sample composition.

claim: Homotopic visual areas were highly correlated with a mean of 0.88 and range of area means from 0.85–0.90.
source: Homotopic areas (e.g. left ventral V1 and right ventral V1; diagonal of Figure 1A) were highly correlated (mean [M]=0.88, range of area means: 0.85–0.90)
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values for homotopic areas, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Homotopic areas were more correlated than non-homotopic areas such as the same visual area across streams.
source: Homotopic areas (e.g. left ventral V1 and right ventral V1; diagonal of Figure 1A) were highly correlated (mean [M]=0.88, range of area means: 0.85–0.90), and more correlated than non-homotopic areas, such as the same visual area across streams (e.g. left ventral V1 and right dorsal V1; Figure 1B; ΔFisher Z M=0.42, p<0.001).
evidence: This statement provides a statistical comparison between homotopic and non-homotopic areas with specific values and significance.

claim: There was no evidence that variability in movie duration per participant correlated with the difference in homotopic versus non-homotopic area correlations.
source: We found no evidence that the variability in movie duration per participant correlated with this difference (r=0.08, p=0.700).
evidence: This statement provides a specific correlation value and p-value indicating no relationship.

claim: Within stream, homotopic areas were more correlated than adjacent areas in the visual hierarchy.
source: Within stream (Figure 1C), homotopic areas were more correlated than adjacent areas in the visual hierarchy (e.g. left ventral V1 and right ventral V2; ΔFisher Z M=0.09, p<0.001)
evidence: This statement provides a statistical comparison with specific values and significance, referencing Figure 1C.

claim: Adjacent areas were more correlated than distal areas in the visual hierarchy.
source: adjacent areas were more correlated than distal areas (e.g. left ventral V1 and right ventral V4; ΔFisher Z M=0.20, p<0.001).
evidence: This statement provides a statistical comparison with specific values and significance.

claim: There was no correlation between movie duration and the effect of same versus adjacent area correlations.
source: There was no correlation between movie duration and effect (Same>Adjacent: r=−0.01, p=0.965, Adjacent>Distal: r=−0.09, p=0.740).
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values and p-values indicating no relationship.

claim: Controlling for motion in the correlation between areas results in negligibly different effects.
source: Additionally, if we control for motion in the correlation between areas – in case motion transients drive consistent activity across areas – then the effects described here are negligibly different (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement describes a control analysis with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Movies elicit distinct processing dynamics across areas of infant visual cortex defined independently using retinotopic mapping.
source: Hence, movies elicit distinct processing dynamics across areas of infant visual cortex defined independently using retinotopic mapping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the preceding analyses showing differential correlations across visual areas.

claim: The stress of fitting the cross-correlation matrix data with a two-dimensional MDS was in the acceptable range at 0.076.
source: The stress of fitting these data with a two-dimensional MDS was in the acceptable range (0.076).
evidence: This statement provides a specific stress value for the MDS analysis.

claim: Areas in the adult-defined ventral stream differentiated from areas in the adult-defined dorsal stream in the MDS analysis.
source: Clear organization was present (Figure 2): areas in the adult-defined ventral stream (e.g. VO, PHC) differentiated from areas in the adult-defined dorsal stream (e.g. V3A/B).
evidence: This statement describes the results of the MDS analysis with reference to Figure 2.

claim: There is a slight separation between canonical dorsal areas and the recently defined lateral pathway in the MDS analysis.
source: Indeed, we see a slight separation between canonical dorsal areas and the recently defined lateral pathway (Weiner and Gomez, 2021) (e.g. LO1, hMT), although more evidence is needed to substantiate this distinction.
evidence: This statement describes an observation from the MDS analysis with a citation to support the concept of a lateral pathway.

claim: hV4 and V3A/B represent the same visual space yet have distinct functional profiles.
source: We see that in infants too: hV4 and V3A/B represent the same visual space yet have distinct functional profiles.
evidence: This statement describes a specific finding about the functional profiles of two visual areas.

claim: The organization of ventral and dorsal streams cannot be attributed to mere spatial autocorrelation within stream because analyses were conducted across hemispheres.
source: Again, this organization cannot be attributed to mere spatial autocorrelation within stream because analyses were conducted across hemispheres (at significant anatomical distance) and this pattern is preserved when accounting for motion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement provides reasoning for why spatial autocorrelation is not a confound, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The results provide evidence of a dissociation in the functional profile of anatomically defined ventral and dorsal streams during infant movie-watching.
source: These results thus provide evidence of a dissociation in the functional profile of anatomically defined ventral and dorsal streams during infant movie-watching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MDS analysis results.

claim: Across infant participants, an average of 2.4 components (range: 0–5) were identified as potential spatial frequency maps.
source: Across infant participants, we identified an average of 2.4 (range: 0–5) components as potential spatial frequency maps
evidence: This statement provides specific values for the number of components identified.

claim: Across infant participants, an average of 1.1 components (range: 0–4) were identified as potential meridian maps.
source: we identified an average of 2.4 (range: 0–5) components as potential spatial frequency maps and 1.1 (range: 0–4) components as potential meridian maps.
evidence: This statement provides specific values for the number of components identified.

claim: Lines drawn parallel to area boundaries show monotonic gradients on spatial frequency maps, with stronger responses to high spatial frequency at the fovea and stronger responses to low spatial frequencies in the periphery.
source: Lines drawn parallel to area boundaries show monotonic gradients on spatial frequency maps, with stronger responses to high spatial frequency at the fovea, and stronger responses to low spatial frequencies in the periphery (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement describes the expected pattern of spatial frequency maps with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Lines drawn perpendicular to area boundaries show oscillations in sensitivity to horizontal and vertical meridians on meridian maps.
source: By contrast, lines drawn perpendicular to the area boundaries show oscillations in sensitivity to horizontal and vertical meridians on meridian maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement describes the expected pattern of meridian maps with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The absolute correlations between the task-evoked maps and the manually identified spatial frequency components had a mean of 0.52 and range of 0.23–0.85.
source: Figure 4A shows the absolute correlations between the task-evoked maps and the manually identified spatial frequency components (M=0.52, range: 0.23–0.85).
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The best spatial frequency component was identified in 6 of 13 participants.
source: We identified the best component in 6 of 13 participants (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement provides a specific count of successful identifications with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The percentile of the average manually identified spatial frequency component was high (M=63.8 percentile, range: 26.7–98.1) and significantly above chance.
source: The percentile of the average manually identified component was high (M=63.8 percentile, range: 26.7–98.1) and significantly above chance (ΔM=13.8, CI=[3.3–24.0], p=0.011).
evidence: This statement provides specific percentile values and statistical significance.

claim: The manually identified components derived from movie-watching data are similar to the spatial frequency maps derived from retinotopic mapping.
source: This illustrates that the manually identified components derived from movie-watching data are similar to the spatial frequency maps derived from retinotopic mapping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation and percentile analyses.

claim: The underlying architecture of the infant visual system influences how movies are processed.
source: The fact that this can work also indicates the underlying architecture of the infant visual system influences how movies are processed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the success of identifying spatial frequency maps from movie data.

claim: The correlation between the task-evoked meridian maps and the manually identified components had a mean of 0.46 and range of 0.03–0.81.
source: Figure 4C shows the correlation between the task-evoked meridian maps and the manually identified components (M=0.46, range: 0.03–0.81).
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The best possible meridian component was identified for 1 out of 9 participants.
source: Compared to all possible components identified by ICA, the best possible component was identified for 1 out of 9 participants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement provides a specific count of successful identifications with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The percentile of the average manually identified meridian component was numerically high (M=67.6 percentile, range: 3.0–100.0) but not significantly above chance.
source: Although the percentile of the average manually identified component was numerically high (M=67.6 percentile, range: 3.0–100.0), it was not significantly above chance (ΔM=17.6, CI=[–1.8–33.0], p=0.074).
evidence: This statement provides specific percentile values and statistical non-significance.

claim: Spatial frequency maps have a coarser structure than meridian maps and are more invariant to fixation, which may explain why they are easier to identify.
source: Spatial frequency maps have a coarser structure than meridian maps, and are more invariant to fixation, which may explain why they are easier to identify.
evidence: This statement provides a speculative explanation for the difference in identification success between map types.

claim: In 6 participants without visible clues in rolled data, only 1 of the 14 components labeled as spatial frequency or meridian from 920 total components was a rolled component.
source: In the 6 participants without such clues, only 1 of the 14 components labeled as spatial frequency or meridian, from 920 total components, was a rolled component.
evidence: This statement provides specific counts from the control analysis.

claim: The fact that 13 of 14 selected components (93%) were original was extremely unlikely to have occurred by chance (binomial test: p=0.002).
source: The fact that 13 of 14 selected components (93%) were original was extremely unlikely to have occurred by chance (binomial test: p=0.002).
evidence: This statement provides a specific statistical test result.

claim: The selection procedure rarely identified components as retinotopic in realistic noise.
source: Thus, our selection procedure rarely identified components as retinotopic in realistic noise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rolled component control analysis.

claim: The expanded dataset included 71 movie-watching datasets from additional infants who saw the same movies but did not have usable retinotopy data.
source: These analyses also benefit from greater amounts of data, so we expanded the sample in two ways (Appendix 1—table 3): First, we added 71 movie-watching datasets from additional infants who saw the same movies but did not have usable retinotopy data (and thus were not included in the analyses above that compared movie and retinotopy data within participant).
evidence: This statement describes the expansion of the dataset for SRM analyses.

claim: The expanded dataset included data from 8 adult participants who completed the retinotopy task and saw a subset of the movies shown to infants.
source: Second, we used data from adult participants, including 8 participants who completed the retinotopy task and saw a subset of the movies we showed infants
evidence: This statement describes the inclusion of adult participants in the expanded dataset.

claim: The expanded dataset included 41 datasets from adults who had seen the movies shown to infants but did not have retinotopy data.
source: and 41 datasets from adults who had seen the movies shown to infants but did not have retinotopy data.
evidence: This statement describes the inclusion of additional adult participants in the expanded dataset.

claim: The number of features in the shared space (K=10) was determined via a cross-validation procedure on movie-watching data in adults.
source: The number of features in the shared space (K=10) was determined via a cross-validation procedure on movie-watching data in adults (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement describes the method for determining the number of features in the SRM with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: When using infants to predict a held-out infant, the spatial frequency map predictions are moderately correlated with task-evoked retinotopy data (M=0.46, range: –0.06 to 0.78).
source: When using the infants to predict a held-out infant, the spatial frequency map (Figure 6A) and meridian map (Figure 6C) predictions are moderately correlated with task-evoked retinotopy data (spatial frequency: M=0.46, range: –0.06 to 0.78
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values for SRM predictions with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: When using infants to predict a held-out infant, the meridian map predictions are moderately correlated with task-evoked retinotopy data (M=0.24, range: –0.12 to 0.78).
source: When using the infants to predict a held-out infant, the spatial frequency map (Figure 6A) and meridian map (Figure 6C) predictions are moderately correlated with task-evoked retinotopy data (spatial frequency: M=0.46, range: –0.06 to 0.78; meridian: M=0.24, range: –0.12 to 0.78).
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values for SRM predictions with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Flipping the held-out participant's movie data significantly worsened prediction of the spatial frequency map (ΔFisher Z M=0.52, CI=[0.24–0.80], p<0.001).
source: Indeed, flipping significantly worsened prediction of the spatial frequency map (ΔFisher Z M=0.52, CI=[0.24–0.80], p<0.001)
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values for the control analysis.

claim: Flipping the held-out participant's movie data significantly worsened prediction of the meridian map (ΔFisher Z M=0.24, CI=[0.02–0.49], p=0.034).
source: Indeed, flipping significantly worsened prediction of the spatial frequency map (ΔFisher Z M=0.52, CI=[0.24–0.80], p<0.001) and the meridian map (ΔFisher Z M=0.24, CI=[0.02–0.49], p=0.034).
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values for the control analysis.

claim: The movie-evoked response enables the mapping of other infants' retinotopic maps into a held-out infant.
source: Hence, the movie-evoked response enables the mapping of other infants' retinotopic maps into a held-out infant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis results.

claim: Using adult data to predict infant data results in maps similar to task-evoked spatial frequency maps (M=0.56, range: 0.17–0.79).
source: Using adult data to predict infant data also results in maps similar to task-evoked spatial frequency maps (Figure 6B; M=0.56, range: 0.17–0.79)
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values for SRM predictions using adult data with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Using adult data to predict infant data results in maps similar to task-evoked meridian maps (M=0.34, range: –0.27–0.64).
source: Using adult data to predict infant data also results in maps similar to task-evoked spatial frequency maps (Figure 6B; M=0.56, range: 0.17–0.79) and meridian maps (Figure 6D; M=0.34, range: –0.27–0.64).
evidence: This statement provides specific correlation values for SRM predictions using adult data with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Flipping the held-out participant's movie data significantly worsened prediction of the spatial frequency map when using adult training data (ΔFisher Z M=0.40, CI=[0.17–0.65], p<0.001).
source: Again, flipping the held-out participants movie data significantly worsened prediction of the held-out participant's spatial frequency map (ΔFisher Z M=0.40, CI=[0.17–0.65], p<0.001)
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values for the control analysis using adult training data.

claim: Flipping the held-out participant's movie data significantly worsened prediction of the meridian map when using adult training data (ΔFisher Z M=0.33, CI=[0.12–0.55], p=0.002).
source: Again, flipping the held-out participants movie data significantly worsened prediction of the held-out participant's spatial frequency map (ΔFisher Z M=0.40, CI=[0.17–0.65], p<0.001) and meridian map (ΔFisher Z M=0.33, CI=[0.12–0.55], p=0.002).
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values for the control analysis using adult training data.

claim: There was no significant difference in SRM performance when using adults versus infants as the training set for spatial frequency maps.
source: There was no significant difference in SRM performance when using adults versus infants as the training set (spatial frequency: ΔFisher Z M=0.14, CI=[–0.00–0.27], p=0.054
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing SRM performance between training sets.

claim: There was no significant difference in SRM performance when using adults versus infants as the training set for meridian maps.
source: There was no significant difference in SRM performance when using adults versus infants as the training set (spatial frequency: ΔFisher Z M=0.14, CI=[–0.00–0.27], p=0.054; meridian: ΔFisher Z M=0.11, CI=[–0.05–0.28], p=0.179).
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing SRM performance between training sets.

claim: SRM could be used to predict visual maps with moderate accuracy.
source: In sum, SRM could be used to predict visual maps with moderate accuracy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis results.

claim: Functional alignment methods like SRM can partially capture the retinotopic organization of visual cortex from infant movie-watching data.
source: This indicates that functional alignment methods like SRM can partially capture the retinotopic organization of visual cortex from infant movie-watching data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis results.

claim: Anatomical alignment of retinotopic maps is significantly better than functional alignment using infants to predict spatial frequency maps.
source: These correlations (Appendix 1—table 4) are significantly higher than for functional alignment (using infants to predict spatial frequency, anatomical alignment<functional alignment: ΔFisher Z M=0.44, CI=[0.32–0.58], p<0.001
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Anatomical alignment of retinotopic maps is significantly better than functional alignment using infants to predict meridian maps.
source: using infants to predict meridians, anatomical alignment<functional alignment: ΔFisher Z M=0.61, CI=[0.47–0.74], p<0.001
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Anatomical alignment of retinotopic maps is significantly better than functional alignment using adults to predict spatial frequency maps.
source: using adults to predict spatial frequency, anatomical alignment<functional alignment: ΔFisher Z M=0.31, CI=[0.21–0.42], p<0.001
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Anatomical alignment of retinotopic maps is significantly better than functional alignment using adults to predict meridian maps.
source: using adults to predict meridians, anatomical alignment<functional alignment: ΔFisher Z M=0.49, CI=[0.39–0.60], p<0.001
evidence: This statement provides specific statistical values comparing anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Even if SRM shows that movies can be used to produce retinotopic maps that are significantly similar to a participant, these maps are not as good as those that can be produced by anatomical alignment of the maps from other participants without any movie data.
source: This suggests that even if SRM shows that movies can be used to produce retinotopic maps that are significantly similar to a participant, these maps are not as good as those that can be produced by anatomical alignment of the maps from other participants without any movie data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Movies evoke activity in infants and toddlers that recapitulate the organization of the visual cortex.
source: In conclusion, movies evoke activity in infants and toddlers that recapitulate the organization of the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the entire study.

claim: Movie-evoked activity is differentiated across visual areas and contains information about the visual maps at the foundation of visual processing.
source: This activity is differentiated across visual areas and contains information about the visual maps at the foundation of visual processing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the entire study.

claim: The movie-evoked response in a visual area is more similar to the same area in the other hemisphere than to different areas in the other hemisphere.
source: We show that the movie-evoked response in a visual area is more similar to the same area in the other hemisphere than to different areas in the other hemisphere.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the homotopy analysis results.

claim: Visual areas are functionally differentiated in infancy and this function is shared across hemispheres.
source: This suggests that visual areas are functionally differentiated in infancy and that this function is shared across hemispheres (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the homotopy analysis with a citation for support.

claim: The greater across-hemisphere similarity for same versus different areas provides some of the first evidence that visual areas and streams are functionally differentiated in infants as young as 5 months of age.
source: The greater across-hemisphere similarity for same versus different areas provides some of the first evidence that visual areas and streams are functionally differentiated in infants as young as 5 months of age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the homotopy analysis results.

claim: Previous work suggests that functions of the dorsal and ventral streams are detectable in young infants but that the localization of these functions is immature.
source: Previous work suggests that functions of the dorsal and ventral streams are detectable in young infants (Wattam-Bell et al., 2010) but that the localization of these functions is immature (Braddick and Atkinson, 2011).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior research with citations.

claim: The areas of infant visual cortex that will mature into the dorsal and ventral streams have distinct activity profiles during movie-watching.
source: Despite this, we find that the areas of infant visual cortex that will mature into the dorsal and ventral streams have distinct activity profiles during movie-watching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results in the context of prior research.

claim: Movies evoke differentiated activity in the infant visual cortex between areas.
source: Not only do movies evoke differentiated activity in the infant visual cortex between areas, but movies also evoke fine-grained information about the organization of maps within areas.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study findings.

claim: Movies evoke fine-grained information about the organization of maps within areas.
source: Not only do movies evoke differentiated activity in the infant visual cortex between areas, but movies also evoke fine-grained information about the organization of maps within areas.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study findings.

claim: Components were observed that were highly similar to a spatial frequency map obtained from the same infant in a retinotopy task.
source: We observed components that were highly similar to a spatial frequency map obtained from the same infant in a retinotopy task.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the ICA analysis results.

claim: The retinotopic organization of the infant brain accounts for a detectable amount of variance in visual activity.
source: This means that the retinotopic organization of the infant brain accounts for a detectable amount of variance in visual activity, otherwise components resembling these maps would not be discoverable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ICA analysis results.

claim: The components could be identified without knowledge of the ground-truth maps; however, their moderate similarity to the task-defined maps makes them a poor replacement.
source: Importantly, the components could be identified without knowledge of these ground-truth maps; however, their moderate similarity to the task-defined maps makes them a poor replacement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ICA analysis results.

claim: Although some of the components are similar to a spatial frequency map or meridian map, they could reflect a different kind of visual map.
source: One caveat for interpreting these results is that although some of the components are similar to a spatial frequency map or meridian map, they could reflect a different kind of visual map.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the ICA results.

claim: The spatial frequency map is highly correlated with the eccentricity map.
source: For instance, the spatial frequency map is highly correlated with the eccentricity map (Henriksson et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2001; Srihasam et al., 2014; Tolhurst and Thompson, 1981, which itself is related to receptive field size).
evidence: This statement describes a known relationship between map types with citations.

claim: It is inappropriate to make strong claims about the underlying function of the components based on their similarity to visual maps alone.
source: This means it is inappropriate to make strong claims about the underlying function of the components based on their similarity to visual maps alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of the ICA analysis.

claim: ICA does not provide a scale to the variation in the components.
source: Another limitation is that ICA does not provide a scale to the variation: although we find a correlation between gradients of spatial frequency in the ground truth and the selected component, we cannot use the component alone to infer the spatial frequency selectivity of any part of cortex.
evidence: This statement describes a limitation of the ICA method.

claim: It is possible to discover approximations of visual maps in infants and toddlers with movie-watching data and ICA.
source: Nonetheless, these results do show that it is possible to discover approximations of visual maps in infants and toddlers with movie-watching data and ICA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ICA analysis results.

claim: Success with the SRM approach means that visual maps are engaged during infant movie-watching.
source: Hence, success with this approach means that visual maps are engaged during infant movie-watching.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SRM analysis results.

claim: This result shows that functional alignment is practical for studies in awake infants that produce small amounts of data.
source: Furthermore, this result shows that functional alignment is practical for studies in awake infants that produce small amounts of data (Ellis and Turk-Browne, 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis results with a citation.

claim: This is initial evidence that functional alignment may be useful for enhancing signal quality or revealing changing function over development.
source: This is initial evidence that functional alignment may be useful for enhancing signal quality, like it has in adults (Busch et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2015; Guntupalli et al., 2016), or revealing changing function over development (Yates et al., 2021), which may prove especially useful for infant fMRI (Ellis and Turk-Browne, 2018).
evidence: This statement speculates about future applications with citations for support.

claim: Movies evoke sufficiently reliable activity across infants and adults to find a shared response, and this shared response contains information about the organization of infant visual cortex.
source: In sum, movies evoke sufficiently reliable activity across infants and adults to find a shared response, and this shared response contains information about the organization of infant visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the SRM analysis.

claim: Movies do not work well enough to replace a retinotopy task when accurate maps are needed.
source: To be clear, we are not suggesting that movies work well enough to replace a retinotopy task when accurate maps are needed.
evidence: This is a clarification about the limitations of movie-based mapping.

claim: Without knowing the ground truth from a retinotopy task, there would be no way to weed out components with lower correlations.
source: For instance, even though ICA found components that were highly correlated with the spatial frequency map, we also selected some components that turned out to have lower correlations. Without knowing the ground truth from a retinotopy task, there would be no way to weed these out.
evidence: This statement describes a limitation of the ICA approach.

claim: Anatomical alignment resulted in maps that were highly similar to the ground truth.
source: Additionally, anatomical alignment (i.e. averaging the maps from other participants and anatomically aligning them to a held-out participant) resulted in maps that were highly similar to the ground truth.
evidence: This statement describes the results of the anatomical alignment analysis.

claim: Adult-defined visual areas were moderately similar to infants in a previous study.
source: Indeed, we previously Ellis et al., 2021 found that adult-defined visual areas were moderately similar to infants.
evidence: This statement references a finding from a prior study with a citation.

claim: In adults, functional alignment can outperform anatomical alignment methods in similar analyses.
source: While functional alignment with adults can outperform anatomical alignment methods in similar analyses (Guntupalli et al., 2016), here we find that functional alignment is inferior to anatomical alignment.
evidence: This statement contrasts findings in adults with the current study results, with a citation.

claim: If the goal is to define visual areas in an infant that lacks task-based retinotopy, anatomical alignment of other participants' retinotopic maps is superior to using movie-based analyses.
source: Thus, if the goal is to define visual areas in an infant that lacks task-based retinotopy, anatomical alignment of other participants' retinotopic maps is superior to using movie-based analyses, at least as we tested it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of anatomical and functional alignment.

claim: Participants looked at the screen for an average of 93.7% of the time (range: 78–99) for the movies used in the homotopy analyses and ICA.
source: Participants looked at the screen for an average of 93.7% of the time (range: 78–99) for the movies used in the homotopy analyses and ICA
evidence: This statement provides specific gaze coding data.

claim: Participants looked at the screen for an average of 94.5% of the time (range: 82–99) for the movies used in the SRM analyses.
source: and 94.5% of the time (range: 82–99) for the movies used in the SRM analyses (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This statement provides specific gaze coding data.

claim: The mammalian visual cortex is divided into multiple areas with partially distinct functional roles between areas.
source: The mammalian visual cortex is divided into multiple areas with partially distinct functional roles between areas (Brodmann, 1909; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about visual cortex organization with citations.

claim: Within visual areas, there are orderly, topographic representations, or maps, of visual space.
source: Within visual areas, there are orderly, topographic representations, or maps, of visual space (Kaas, 1997; White and Fitzpatrick, 2007).
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about visual cortex organization with citations.

claim: Visual maps capture information about the location and spatial extent of visual stimuli with respect to fixation.
source: These maps capture information about the location and spatial extent of visual stimuli with respect to fixation.
evidence: This statement describes the function of visual maps based on established knowledge.

claim: Visual maps reflect sensitivity to polar angle, measured via alternations between horizontal and vertical meridians that define area boundaries.
source: Thus, maps reflect sensitivity to polar angle, measured via alternations between horizontal and vertical meridians that define area boundaries (Fox et al., 1987; Schneider et al., 1993)
evidence: This statement describes a property of visual maps with citations.

claim: Visual maps reflect sensitivity to spatial frequency, reflected in gradients of sensitivity to high and low spatial frequencies from foveal to peripheral vision, respectively.
source: and sensitivity to spatial frequency, reflected in gradients of sensitivity to high and low spatial frequencies from foveal to peripheral vision, respectively (Henriksson et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement describes a property of visual maps with a citation.

claim: Visual maps could be revealed by a retinotopy task in infants as young as 5 months of age in a previous study.
source: Previously, we reported that these maps could be revealed by a retinotopy task in infants as young as 5 months of age (Ellis et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement references a finding from a prior study with a citation.

claim: It remains unclear whether visual maps are evoked by more naturalistic task designs.
source: However, it remains unclear whether these maps are evoked by more naturalistic task designs.

claim: Movies drive strong and naturalistic responses in sensory regions while minimizing task demands.
source: Movies drive strong and naturalistic responses in sensory regions while minimizing task demands (Loiotile et al., 2019; Nastase et al., 2020; Finn et al., 2022) and thus are a proxy for typical experience.
evidence: This statement describes a property of movie stimuli with citations.

claim: In adults, movies and resting-state data have been used to characterize the visual cortex in a data-driven fashion.
source: In adults, movies and resting-state data have been used to characterize the visual cortex in a data-driven fashion (Knapen, 2021; Lu et al., 2017; Guntupalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement describes prior research in adults with citations.

claim: Movies have been useful in awake infant fMRI for studying event segmentation, functional alignment, and brain networks.
source: Movies have been useful in awake infant fMRI for studying event segmentation (Yates et al., 2022), functional alignment (Turek et al., 2018), and brain networks (Yates et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement describes prior research in infants with citations.

claim: Past work with movies in infants did not address the granularity and specificity of cortical organization that movies evoke.
source: However, this past work did not address the granularity and specificity of cortical organization that movies evoke.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in prior research that the current study addresses.

claim: Movies evoke similar activity across infants in anatomically aligned visual areas.
source: For example, movies evoke similar activity across infants in anatomically aligned visual areas (Yates et al., 2022)
evidence: This statement references a finding from a prior study with a citation.

claim: It remains unclear whether responses to movie content differ between visual areas.
source: but it remains unclear whether responses to movie content differ between visual areas (e.g. is there more similarity of function within visual areas than between [Li et al., 2022]).

claim: It is unknown whether structure within visual areas, namely visual maps, contributes substantially to visual-evoked activity.
source: Moreover, it is unknown whether structure within visual areas, namely visual maps, contributes substantially to visual-evoked activity.

claim: Functional alignment finds a mapping between participants using functional activity rather than anatomy.
source: Functional alignment finds a mapping between participants using functional activity – rather than anatomy
evidence: This statement describes the concept of functional alignment.

claim: In adults, functional alignment can improve signal-to-noise, enhance across participant prediction, and enable unique analyses.
source: and in adults can improve signal-to-noise, enhance across participant prediction, and enable unique analyses (Busch et al., 2021; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2020b).

claim: Movies may not fully sample the stimulus parameters or visual functions needed to find topographic maps and areas in visual cortex.
source: Nonetheless, there are several reasons for skepticism that movies could evoke detailed, retinotopic organization: Movies may not fully sample the stimulus parameters (e.g. spatial frequencies) or visual functions needed to find topographic maps and areas in visual cortex.
evidence: This statement presents a potential limitation of using movies for retinotopic mapping.

claim: Even if movies contain the necessary visual properties, they may unfold at a faster rate than can be detected by fMRI.
source: Even if movies contain the necessary visual properties, they may unfold at a faster rate than can be detected by fMRI.
evidence: This statement presents a potential limitation of using movies for retinotopic mapping.

claim: Naturalistic stimuli may not drive visual responses as robustly as experimenter-defined stimuli that are designed for retinotopic mapping with discrete onsets and high contrast.
source: Additionally, naturalistic stimuli may not drive visual responses as robustly as experimenter-defined stimuli that are designed for retinotopic mapping with discrete onsets and high contrast.
evidence: This statement presents a potential limitation of using movies for retinotopic mapping.

claim: The complexity of movie stimuli may result in variable attention between participants, impeding discovery of reliable visual structure across individuals.
source: Finally, the complexity of movie stimuli may result in variable attention between participants, impeding discovery of reliable visual structure across individuals.
evidence: This statement presents a potential limitation of using movies for retinotopic mapping.

claim: If movies do show the fine-grained organization of the infant visual cortex, this suggests that this structure scaffolds the processing of ongoing visual information.
source: If movies do show the fine-grained organization of the infant visual cortex, this suggests that this structure (e.g. visual maps) scaffolds the processing of ongoing visual information.
